You’re right. I should have explained the finding before editing.

**The bug:** PR #2370 correctly excludes remotes that have only a `pushurl`, but its new lookup uses `git config --local --get-regexp` without `--includes`. Git can use a `fork` remote defined through `.git/config`’s `include.path`, while this lookup cannot see it. An explicit `checkpoint_push_remote: fork` then fails with a false “no configured fetch URL” error. Automatic capture also skips `fork`. This is the [reviewer’s comment](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2370#discussion_r4082827415).

**My proposed fix:** add `--includes` to the local config lookup, update its scope comments, and verify that explicit election and automatic capture accept an included remote while the existing `pushurl`-only cases remain excluded. I would keep `--local`: expanding the scan to all config scopes could change which remote wins by default.

Yes. The [review comment](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2370#discussion_r4082827415) proposes two alternatives:

1. Add `--includes` to the existing `git config --local --get-regexp` call.
2. Keep that list unchanged and check named remotes separately with `git config --get-all remote.<name>.url`.

It also asks for an included-remote regression test and an update to the cache comment. I chose the first option in the uncommitted edits because it fixes the reported `include.path` case with a smaller change.
so tell me what is happening here? what bug we fixed and what new bug it caused?

The original bug was about a remote that could **receive a push but could not be used to read checkpoints back**:

```ini
[remote "pushonly"]
    pushurl = https://example.com/repo.git
    # no url
```

The old eligibility check used `git remote get-url`. For this configuration, that check could succeed, so Entire might elect `pushonly` for checkpoint sync even though it had no fetch URL. The PR fixed that by electing only remotes found through `remote.*.url`.

That introduced the new bug. Git allows a valid remote URL to live in a file referenced by `.git/config`:

```ini
[include]
    path = /path/to/remotes.cfg
```

Git can see and use a `fork` remote in that file. But the PR’s lookup runs `git config --local --get-regexp` **without `--includes`**, so Entire’s eligibility list misses `fork`. An explicit `checkpoint_push_remote: fork` now fails with an incorrect “no configured fetch URL” error; automatic capture can miss it too.

So the rule in the PR is right, but the command collecting eligible remotes reads too little of Git’s config. Adding `--includes` lets it see valid included fetch URLs while still excluding remotes with only a `pushurl`.
wait i didn't understand any of this. explain in simple terms.

Think of a Git remote as a saved address. Entire needs an address it can use to **send checkpoints and read them back**.

- **Original bug:** A remote had only a “send” address. Entire treated it as usable, sent checkpoints there, then could not read them back.
- **PR fix:** Require a “read” address before choosing a remote.
- **New bug:** Some people keep that read address in a second Git settings file. Git reads the second file, but the PR’s new check does not. Entire wrongly says the remote has no read address and refuses to use it.

The reviewer’s suggested `--includes` option tells the check to read that second file too.
okay so in real terms what's happening?

Imagine you work on a fork. You’ve told Entire, “Send my checkpoints to `fork`.” Git knows the address for `fork`, but you keep that address in a separate config file linked from `.git/config`.

You run `git push fork`. **Git finds the address and pushes your code.** With this PR, **Entire fails to find the same address**, says `fork` has no fetch URL, and skips checkpoint sync. Your code arrives; your checkpoints stay local.

Why did the PR add this check? Before it, Entire could choose a remote with only a push address. It could send checkpoints there but could not fetch them back. The PR correctly rejects those remotes. It accidentally also rejects valid remotes whose address is in an included config file.

The proposed change makes Entire read that included file, just as Git does.
you keep that address in a separate config file linked from .git/config. ohh so this is possible that people keep the fork linked to config somewhere else? what is the scenario here?

Yes. Git lets `.git/config` point to another config file, and treats the settings in that file as part of the repository’s configuration. For example:

```ini
# .git/config
[include]
    path = /Users/alice/.config/git/project-remotes
```

```ini
# project-remotes
[remote "fork"]
    url = git@github.com:alice/project.git
```

Alice or a setup tool might keep her personal remote settings in that separate file. `git push fork` works because Git reads both files.

It’s less common than `git remote add fork`, but it’s a supported setup. The regression is that Git sees `fork` while Entire’s new check sees only the first file.
that's because entire only reads .git/config and not any other config in user's file right?

Yes, for **this particular check**. Entire asks Git to read `.git/config`, but the command it uses does not follow that file’s `include.path` link. So it misses a remote stored in the linked file, even though normal Git commands can see it.

The proposed `--includes` flag makes this check follow files linked from `.git/config`. An unrelated global Git config file is a separate case.
okay but that file can have other configs too but entire is local first so we should not be worried about anything right?

Mostly, yes, but one detail matters: `--local` limits the **config scope**; it does not mean `.git/config` always wins before an included file.

With `--includes`, this check still looks only for remote fetch addresses (`remote.*.url`). It ignores unrelated settings in the file. Included remotes do join Entire’s choice of checkpoint remote, though. If there’s no explicit choice or `origin`, their order could affect which remote is chosen by default. That’s the behavior I’d verify alongside the reported fix.
